title: Identification and Estimation of Treatment Effects with a Regression Discontinuity Design
research_question: Does an integrated anti-poverty program that conditions cash transfers and nutritional supplements on children's school attendance and health-clinic visits improve the welfare of poor rural households, including their education, health, nutrition, and consumption outcomes?
data_description: The evaluation uses panel survey data collected by IFPRI on approximately 24,000 households drawn from 506 localities across 7 Mexican states, with repeated household interviews conducted periodically between November 1997 and November 1999. Key outcome variables span school enrollment (especially at the secondary level), child labor, illness incidence and disability days for children and adults, child stunting for those aged 12–36 months, caloric intake, and dietary diversity (including fruits, vegetables, and meat consumption). The data are complemented by qualitative information from focus groups and workshops with beneficiaries, local leaders, program officials, health clinic workers, and schoolteachers, as well as administrative cost data on program operations. The unit of observation is the rural household, with children and adults as additional units for specific human-capital outcomes.
institutional_context: PROGRESA was a major Mexican federal anti-poverty program launched in the late 1990s with a 1999 budget near $777 million (0.2% of GDP), reaching about 2.6 million families in roughly 50,000 localities by year-end 1999—about 40% of rural Mexican families. The program combined education, health, and nutrition interventions into one package, channeling cash transfers and nutritional supplements exclusively to mothers conditional on children's school attendance and health-center visits. Targeting operated in two stages: marginal communities were selected from census-based economic indices, and within those communities, eligible households were identified using socioeconomic data. Crucially, program rollout was phased: some eligible localities received benefits earlier while others were incorporated later, generating treatment and not-yet-treated comparison groups that IFPRI used as the basis for its evaluation beginning in early 1998.
